Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, the appraisal that the patient's own body has been permanently damaged is hard to reconcile unless the patient was also directly physically injured; that direct-injury theme is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: Threat items center on personal physical danger and hypervigilance in the environment ('back to wall', exaggerated startle), which fits direct personal assault/combat trauma more than trauma to a loved one, and is not well linked to the reported appraisal content.

issues.item: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, this item implies an ongoing need to guard against immediate external danger to oneself. That does not fit well with the rest of the profile, which centers on bereavement-related cognitions (survival guilt, numbness) rather than personal threat exposure. It is also weakly aligned with the formulation, where Threat is linked mainly with Negative Appraisals and not with trigger-driven hyperarousal or ongoing danger monitoring.

The threat items are dominated by nonspecific hyperarousal and reminder reactivity, which usually implies trigger-linked activation, but the formulation specifies Triggers → Threat as inactive. With no trigger content present, 'physical reactions when reminded' is poorly aligned with the stated formulation structure.

'Mistrust: People can't be trusted' is a broad interpersonal appraisal that is not well anchored to trauma to a loved one in the rest of this profile. The other appraisal items center on guilt and emotional deadness, but pervasive mistrust suggests a different trauma pattern and lacks support from the selected threat items.

vignette:
Kai, a 60-year-old South Eastern Asian American fisherman, sat across from me, his weathered hands clasped tightly, a lifetime of sun and sea etched onto his face. He spoke softly, recounting the day five years ago that had fundamentally altered his world. It was a sudden, violent squall that had swept over their small fishing vessel, a storm that rose from nowhere, swallowing his younger brother and fishing partner, Linh, whole. Kai had been pulled from the churning waters by another boat, barely alive, while Linh was never found. The memory of the ocean’s ferocity and the desperate, futile cries of his brother haunted him, a constant, low thrum beneath the surface of his days.

In the aftermath, a profound sense of survival guilt had taken root in Kai’s heart; he felt deeply that he had no right to be alive when Linh was gone, a pervasive belief that whispered, "I feel guilty for surviving when others did not." This guilt, heavy and unrelenting, began to shape his perception of the world. He started to feel a profound mistrust, a growing conviction that "people can't be trusted"—not the meteorologists whose forecasts had been so wrong, not the sea that had betrayed them, and certainly not himself, for failing to save Linh. This deepening sense of mistrust and his overwhelming guilt became a constant lens through which he viewed his life, contributing to an increasing physical reactivity. A sudden shift in the wind while out on the water, or the unexpected thrum of another boat’s engine, would send a jolt through him, his heart pounding in his chest, his muscles tensing as if bracing for another unseen blow. These physical responses were often accompanied by waves of intense negative emotions, primarily fear and a searing horror, as if the past was replaying itself in real-time.

Over the years, this constant state of vigilance and emotional distress began to feed back into his core beliefs. The frequent episodes of physical reactivity—the racing heart, the sudden cold sweats, the overwhelming sense of dread triggered by the most mundane reminders of the sea—only seemed to confirm his mistrust. He reasoned that if his body was constantly screaming danger, then the world truly was an unpredictable and untrustworthy place. His nights offered little respite; he experienced persistent sleep problems, struggling to fall asleep and waking frequently, often drenched in sweat from nightmares. The exhaustion from this chronic insomnia left him feeling utterly depleted, further intensifying his sense of emotional numbness. He described it as "I feel dead inside," a protective shell that had grown thick and impenetrable, making it difficult to connect with his wife, Mai, or find joy in his grandchildren. This numbness, in turn, reinforced his belief that he was permanently broken, a mere shell of his former self, undeserving of peace.

His work as a fisherman, once his passion, became a daily ordeal. The docks, the smell of salt and diesel, the ceaseless rocking of his boat—all were potent reminders. He found himself avoiding deep-sea fishing, sticking to the calmer, safer coastal waters, which significantly impacted his income. What frightened him most was the increasing social isolation; he stopped joining his fellow fishermen for their morning coffee, unable to bear their casual talk of the sea, fearing a sudden wave of negative emotions would overwhelm him. Mai, worried by his increasing withdrawal and the dark circles under his eyes, had finally urged him to seek help, concerned not just for his mental state, but for his physical health. Kai came seeking a way out of the tightening loop of fear and guilt, desperately hoping to feel something other than dread and emptiness, and to finally sleep without the ghost of the storm.
